newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Congress seen agreeing capital gains cut.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Congress seen agreeing capital gains cut.

text.p: When final horse trading ends over this year's federal budget, a capital gains tax cut is expected to be enacted that is more than President Clinton wants to give, but less than Republicans want to receive.

Clinton knows a tax cut on money made from selling investments is high on the Republican wish list in Congress, so he is likely to use it as a trading card to get through some of his priorities, analysts said.

"The president knows the Republicans want capital gains very badly and he can hold that prospect of giving them that and making them pay through the nose to get it," J.D. Foster, executive director of the Tax Foundation, said.
"They (Republicans) have raised the value of this to be very high and it doesn't really cost him (Clinton) that much to give it up, but he can get a great deal for it," he said.
In exchange, Clinton will probably seek less cuts in certain spending areas and most of the tax increases he has proposed, Foster said.
As the real negotiations over Clinton's plan to balance the budget by 2002 begin, differences with Republicans on capital gains are wide.
Clinton's budget includes a capital gains tax cut only for the sale of homes. Republicans want a broad-based cut in rates.
Senate Democrats have issued proposals that offer targeted capital gains tax cuts for small businesses. Settling the differences is not expected to be easy.

A capital gains tax cut is generally a bad idea, Robert McIntyre, director of Citizens for Tax Justice, said. "However you tried to structure it, it would be a big tax cut for people who don't need it," he said.
The Republican plan would mean $10 a year savings for individuals in the middle of the income spectrum and $15,000 a year for individuals in the top 1 percent, McIntyre said.
But others say momentum is behind a capital gains tax cut this year.

The re-election of a Republican Congress and a Democratic president forced the two sides to pledge to work together. Underneath the veneer of bipartisan good will, however, the challenge will be formulating compromise legislation.

After an unusual trip by Clinton to meet with Republican leaders in Congress last month, lawmakers announced with much fanfare that five bipartisan working groups would be formed on priority issues, including taxes. However, the groups have yet to get started.

"I think we'll have, most likely, a three-tiered proposal," Foster said. The final package is likely to include Clinton's tax relief for homeowners, a reduction in the capital gains tax rate to possibly 21 percent from 28 percent, and some tax relief for small businesses, Foster said.

"I will be astonished if we do not have some fairly significant capital gains relief, much more than the president has asked for and less than the Republicans hoped for, but a middle ground which means some sort of general reduction in the rate," Foster said.

John Hilley, White House director of legislative affairs, said the administration would be open to looking at some targeted areas, such as a capital gains tax cut for small businesses, but would be concerned about a broad-based plan.
"One of our concerns, if we were to come around on a capital gains tax proposal, would be to make sure it doesn't explode the deficit outside the budget window," Hilley said.

Clinton's proposal would allow a couple that sells a home to take up to a $500,000 gain tax free every two years. The Republican plan would reduce the maximum rate to 19.8 percent from the current 28 percent.

The congressional Joint Committee on Taxation estimated the cost of Clinton's capital gains tax proposal at about $2.5 billion over five years. The committee, which evaluates tax provisions, put the cost of the Republican capital gains tax cut at about $33.5 billion over five years.
"Is there going to be a capital gains tax cut? The answer is yes," Mark Bloomfield, president of the American Council for Capital Formation, said.

"The president wants to have a balanced budget, and he knows to do that he has to give the Republicans what they want. Therefore, if there is a budget deal, there will be a capital gains tax cut," Bloomfield said.
